section.title: The Lord's Anger against Zion
section.sectionRationale: The second poem lifts its eyes from the ruined city to the hand behind the ruin. Where chapter one wept over what happened, chapter two dares to say who did it: the Lord Himself, in the day of His anger. It is the most unflinching statement in the book that Jerusalem's fall was the deliberate act of God against His own people for their sin, and yet it ends by teaching them to pour out their hearts to that same Lord.
section.thesis: Jerusalem's destruction was no accident of history but the deliberate work of the Lord in righteous anger against His people's sin; yet even the God who wielded the sword is the God to whom the poet directs His people to lift up their hands and pour out their hearts.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Lord as warrior against Zion, tearing down temple, wall, and king, 2:1 to 10; the poet's overwhelming grief at the suffering of the people, especially the starving children, 2:11 to 19; and the closing cry flung back to the Lord who caused it, 2:20 to 22.

units.label: The Lord has become like an enemy

verses.text: How the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His {{aph|anger}}! He has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth. He has abandoned His footstool in the day of His anger.

Without {{chamal|pity}} the Lord has {{bala|swallowed up}} all the dwellings of Jacob. In His wrath He has demolished the fortified cities of the Daughter of Judah. He brought to the ground and defiled her kingdom and its princes.
In fierce anger He has cut off every horn of Israel and withdrawn His right hand at the approach of the enemy. He has burned in Jacob like a flaming fire that consumes everything around it.
He has bent His bow like an enemy; His right hand is positioned. Like a foe He has killed all who were pleasing to the eye; He has poured out His wrath like fire on the tent of the Daughter of Zion.

The Lord is like an enemy; He has {{bala|swallowed up}} Israel. He has swallowed up all her palaces and destroyed her strongholds. He has multiplied mourning and lamentation for the Daughter of Judah.

He has laid waste His tabernacle like a garden booth; He has destroyed His place of meeting. The LORD has made Zion forget her appointed feasts and Sabbaths. In His fierce anger He has despised both king and priest.

The Lord has rejected His altar; He has abandoned His sanctuary; He has delivered the walls of her palaces into the hand of the enemy. They have raised a shout in the house of the LORD as on the day of an appointed feast.

The LORD determined to destroy the wall of the Daughter of Zion. He stretched out a measuring line and did not withdraw His hand from destroying. He made the ramparts and walls lament; together they waste away.

Her gates have sunk into the ground; He has destroyed and shattered their bars. Her king and her princes are exiled among the nations, the law is no more, and even her prophets find no vision from the LORD.
The elders of the Daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence. They have thrown dust on their heads and put on sackcloth. The young women of Jerusalem have bowed their heads to the ground.
My eyes fail from weeping; I am churning within. My heart is poured out in grief over the destruction of the daughter of my people, because children and infants faint in the streets of the city.
They cry out to their mothers: “Where is the grain and wine?” as they faint like the wounded in the streets of the city, as their lives fade away in the arms of their mothers.

What can I say for you? To what can I compare you, O Daughter of Jerusalem? To what can I liken you, that I may console you, O Virgin Daughter of Zion? For your wound is as deep as the sea. Who can ever heal you?
The visions of your prophets were empty and deceptive; they did not expose your guilt to ward off your captivity. The burdens they envisioned for you were empty and misleading.
All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn. They hiss and shake their heads at the Daughter of Jerusalem: “Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?”
All your enemies open their mouths against you. They hiss and gnash their teeth, saying, “We have swallowed her up. This is the day for which we have waited. We have lived to see it!”

The LORD has done what He planned; He has accomplished His decree, which He ordained in days of old; He has overthrown you without {{chamal|pity}}. He has let the enemy gloat over you and exalted the horn of your foes.
The hearts of the people cry out to the Lord. O wall of the Daughter of Zion, let your tears run down like a river day and night. Give yourself no relief, and your eyes no rest.

Arise, cry out in the night from the first watch of the night. Pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord. Lift up your hands to Him for the lives of your children who are fainting from hunger on the corner of every street.

units.label: Look, O LORD, and consider
units.note: the cry flung back to God

verses.text: Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this? Should women eat their offspring, the infants they have nurtured? Should priests and prophets be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?

Both young and old lie together in the dust of the streets. My young men and maidens have fallen by the sword. You have slain them in the day of Your {{aph|anger}}; You have slaughtered them without compassion.
You summoned my terrors on every side, as for the day of an appointed feast. In the day of the LORD's anger no one escaped or survived; my enemy has destroyed those I nurtured and reared.

aph.gloss: Anger, wrath; literally the nose or nostril, from the flaring or hot breathing of anger. The chapter is saturated with it: the cloud of His anger, the day of His anger, His fierce anger. It names God's settled, righteous opposition to sin, not a loss of temper.

chamal.gloss: To spare, to show pity, to hold back. The refrain without pity, in 2:2, 2:17, and 2:21, is chilling precisely because sparing mercy is God's normal way. That He did not spare shows how serious persistent, unrepented sin had become.

bala.gloss: To swallow up, to engulf and destroy without trace. Used repeatedly of the Lord swallowing up Israel's dwellings, palaces, and strongholds, it pictures total, irreversible ruin, the same word the gloating enemies then throw back, we have swallowed her up.

basic.context: If chapter one wept over the ruins, chapter two names who brought them down: the Lord. This is the hardest chapter to read, because verse after verse says that God Himself, in righteous anger, tore down His own city, His temple, His altar, His king. He became, the poet says, like an enemy. The poem does not soften this. Then it turns to the agony on the ground: starving children fainting in the streets, crying to their mothers for bread that is not there. And it ends by flinging the whole horror back to the God who caused it, Look, O LORD, and consider.
basic.hermeneutics: We have to let this chapter be as severe as it is. It refuses the comfort of saying the disaster just happened or that Babylon simply won. It insists God did this, and did it justly, for real sin, including the false prophets who never called the people to repent. But notice where the poem sends its grief: not away from God in bitterness, but straight to God in prayer. The startling lesson is that the same Lord who wounded is the only Lord who can heal, so pour out your heart to Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The word for anger, aph, drenches the chapter: the cloud of His anger, the day of His anger, His fierce anger. It pictures God's hot, settled opposition to sin, not a tantrum. The chilling refrain without pity translates chamal, to spare, the very thing God normally does, now withheld. And again and again the Lord has swallowed up, bala, His people, a word for total ruin that the enemies then gloat back: we have swallowed her up.
basic.typology: The Lord not sparing His own city and pouring out His wrath foreshadows the deeper mystery of the cross, where God did not spare His own Son but delivered Him up for us all. The wound as deep as the sea, with the cry Who can ever heal you, waits for the one by whose wounds we are healed. And the ruined temple points to Christ, the true temple, torn down and raised again.
basic.christ: The unbearable question of this chapter, Who can ever heal you, is answered only in Christ. On the cross God did not spare His own Son, pouring out on Him the anger our sin deserved, so that the wound as deep as the sea could finally be healed. Jesus is the true temple that was destroyed and rebuilt in three days, and the true King who goes into exile, into death, that His people might come home.
basic.god: God is shown as terrifyingly holy and utterly sovereign: nothing here is outside His hand, and His anger against sin is real and just. Yet even this fierce chapter assumes He is approachable, ending in direct appeal to Him. He is not capricious; He does what He planned and said He would do. And the fact that the poem prays to Him at all confesses that mercy is still possible with the God who judged.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 28 warned of exactly this judgment for covenant breaking. Jeremiah 23 exposes the false prophets who said peace when there was no peace. Romans 8 says God did not spare His own Son. John 2 shows Jesus as the temple destroyed and raised. 1 Peter 2 says by His wounds we are healed.
basic.oneStory: This is the sharpest edge of the exile: God Himself judging His people's sin. But even here the door is not shut. The poem drives the grief back to God in prayer, and the whole story runs on to the cross, where God does not spare His own Son, absorbing the anger of this chapter so that the incurable wound can be healed.

context.literary:
The second poem is again an acrostic of twenty-two three-line verses, and again it puts pe before ayin, so verse 16 begins with the enemies' open mouths and verse 17 with the LORD's act. It is built in three movements of different weight. Verses 1 to 9 are a long catalogue in which God is the subject of nearly every verb. Verses 10 to 19 turn to the human scene: silent elders, fainting children, a poet who can no longer weep, a city told how to pray. Verses 20 to 22 are a single address to God.

The catalogue is arranged, not random. It starts at the footstool and tabernacle, moves through festival and Sabbath, and reaches altar and sanctuary, verses 1, 6 and 7. In verses 6 and 9 the three offices that mediated between God and Israel go down together: king, priest and prophet, with the law between them. The chapter's design is to show that the structures through which Israel had lived with God have each been taken apart by God Himself.

The pivot is verses 18 and 19, the only place in the chapter with commands: 'let your tears run down like a river,' 'Arise, cry out in the night,' 'Pour out your heart like water.' The poem does not end in the catalogue of ruin. It instructs the city how to turn grief into speech to God, and verse 20 then opens with the very cry it has just taught, 'Look, O LORD, and consider.'

The last verse closes the ring. The 'day of the LORD's anger' of verse 1 returns in verses 21 and 22, so that the poem ends where it began, with a day on which no one escaped.
context.historical:
The chapter describes the sack of Jerusalem in 586 BC as the end of the institutions of Israel's life. Verse 6 says the LORD 'laid waste His tabernacle like a garden booth.' Isaiah 1:8 had compared the city to a shelter in a vineyard, and the poet means that the temple was as easily removed as a harvest hut. The footstool of verse 1 is the ark, according to Psalm 132:7-8 and 1 Chronicles 28:2. Notably, the ark is never listed among the things carried off in Jeremiah 52:17-23, and Jeremiah 3:16 foretold that people would no longer remember it, so the poem grieves a loss that the record leaves unexplained.

Verse 9 says the king and princes were exiled, which matches Jeremiah 52:9-11 and 52:24-27, and that the law is no more and the prophets find no vision. The false prophets of verse 14 had told the city that peace would hold. Jeremiah 6:14 and 14:13-14 give their message, and Ezekiel 13:10-12 compares it to whitewash smeared over a wall that was about to fall. The people were told what they wished to hear, and Jeremiah 5:31 says they loved it.

The scenes of famine in verses 11 to 12 and 19 to 20 match the siege conditions of Jeremiah 52:6. The women who eat their children are the fulfilment of Leviticus 26:29 and Deuteronomy 28:53, and Jeremiah 19:9 had predicted the same horror in the same words. It was not unheard of in an ancient siege, 2 Kings 6:28-29, but here it is also covenant judgment.

The mourning customs of verse 10, dust on the head, sackcloth, sitting on the ground, silence, were the standard marks of grief in Israel; Job's friends sat in silence on the ground for seven days, Job 2:12-13.
context.canonical:
The chapter is the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 seen from inside. In Deuteronomy 32:23-25 the LORD says He will spend His arrows against His people, and in Jeremiah 21:5 He says He will fight against them Himself. Lamentations 2:4-5 turns those threats into history, and it also reverses the Song of the Sea. Where Exodus 15:3 sings that 'the LORD is a warrior' against Pharaoh, Lamentations 2:4 says He bent His bow 'like an enemy' against Zion, and Isaiah 63:10 had said that rebellion made Him their enemy.

The 'day of the LORD's anger,' verses 1, 21 and 22, is the day of the prophets: Amos 5:18-20, Zephaniah 1:14-15 and 2:2-3. Zephaniah 1:7 even describes the day as a sacrifice with consecrated guests, and Lamentations 2:22 says the LORD summoned terrors on every side as to a feast day. Psalms 44, 74 and 79 are the companion prayers.

The New Testament draws on this chapter at the cross and at the temple. Passers-by shake their heads and scorn, Matthew 27:39-40, as they did over Jerusalem in verse 15. Jesus pronounces 'your house is left to you desolate,' Matthew 23:38, and Luke 1:69 sets a 'horn of salvation' over against the horns cut off in verse 3. The cup of God's fury, which Isaiah 51:17 and 51:22 say Jerusalem drank and would never drink again, is the cup that Jesus prays to be taken from Him, Matthew 26:39.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants his people to stop reading the disaster as the work of a stronger empire or weaker gods and to see it as the act of the LORD they had broken covenant with. That is a hard thing to say, and it is said for a reason. A God who has done this can also be asked to undo it. If Babylon's gods had won, there would be no one to cry to. Only if the LORD is the actor does prayer make sense, and that is why the same poem that says He swallowed up, demolished and cut off ends in direct speech to Him.

He also wants the children seen. The theology of verses 1 to 9 is mounted on the picture of fainting infants in verses 11 and 12, so that no one can discuss the anger of God as an abstraction. And he wants to name the false prophets as the point at which the nation could have been warned, verse 14, so that later generations will test every comforting word against what the LORD has actually said.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is saturated with description of divine anger, and most of it is meant to stay descriptive. The bold phrases, 'like an enemy,' 'without pity,' 'swallowed up,' are the poet's way of saying what judgment felt like for this covenant people at this moment. They are not a template for explaining every disaster in the world. A reader today should not conclude that a particular storm or illness is God's verdict on a particular nation. The poem has the warnings of Leviticus, Deuteronomy and Jeremiah behind it, and it speaks from inside a covenant.

What is prescribed is the instruction of verses 18 and 19: weep, cry out, 'Pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord,' and lift up your hands. This sets the pattern for hearing a hard word. Honest prayer, offered to the very God who has spoken, is the right response. Psalm 62:8 and 1 Peter 5:7 give the same instruction in different words.

debates.question: Is God Himself the destroyer, or did He only permit Babylon to act?

views.label: God is the direct agent
views.case: The poem uses God as the grammatical subject of dozens of verbs and does not name Babylon once in verses 1 to 9. 'The LORD has done what He planned,' verse 17, and 'He has accomplished His decree.' The enemies appear only as the ones who gloat afterwards, verses 7, 16 and 17.

views.label: Babylon is the instrument, God the governor
views.case: Other texts say the same event through human hands: Nebuchadnezzar is 'My servant,' Jeremiah 25:9, and Isaiah 10:5 calls Assyria 'the rod of My anger.' The poet speaks from the standpoint of faith and sums up the cause behind the causes, without denying the army.

views.label: A covenant verdict, not a general theory
views.case: The language belongs to a covenant lawsuit. Zechariah 1:6 says the survivors admitted, 'Just as the LORD of Hosts purposed to do to us according to our ways and deeds, so He has done to us.' The poet is not stating how God acts in every war but reading this one by the terms He announced in advance.

debates.bearing: The three views overlap. The poem insists that nothing happened outside God's hand and also that the event was announced beforehand, and so it asserts His faithfulness to what He said. It does not give a general rule for explaining other suffering.

debates.question: How much blame do the prophets bear in verse 14?

views.label: A large share
views.case: They saw 'empty and deceptive' visions and did not expose the guilt that could have averted the captivity. Jeremiah 14:13-14 and Ezekiel 13:10-12 hold them responsible for telling the city that there would be peace.

views.label: A shared responsibility
views.case: The people wanted to hear peace, Jeremiah 5:31, and a prophet's false comfort answers a demand as well as creates one. The poem names the prophets, but the confession of the city in chapter 1 implicates everyone.

debates.bearing: Leaders carry heavier accountability for what they teach, yet no one is excused by the failure of his teachers. The right response is to measure every message against the word of the LORD that has already been given.

study.originalLanguages:
The horn is a picture the poet uses twice. In verse 3 the LORD 'cut off every horn of Israel,' and in verse 17 He 'exalted the horn of your foes.' A horn in Hebrew, qeren, stands for strength and honour, as in Hannah's song where the LORD will 'exalt the horn of His anointed,' 1 Samuel 2:10. Psalm 132:17 promises a horn for David. The poem therefore describes the loss of Israel's strength and the transfer of it to her enemies in a single image, and Luke 1:69 will later announce a 'horn of salvation' raised up in David's house.

The word for the city's wound in verses 11 and 13 is shever, which means a break or fracture. It is Jeremiah's word: 'For the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am crushed,' Jeremiah 8:21, followed by the question, 'Is there no balm in Gilead?' The question of Lamentations 2:13, 'Who can ever heal you?', uses the verb rapha, which God claims for Himself in Exodus 15:26, 'I am the LORD who heals you,' and which Hosea 6:1 promises, 'He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us.'

Verse 17 says the LORD 'has done what He planned.' The Hebrew verb is zamam, to purpose or devise, which Zechariah 1:6 uses in the same sense. The next clause says He has accomplished His 'decree,' which is the Hebrew for His word or saying, so that the disaster is the carrying out of what He had spoken.

The feast vocabulary is bitter. Mo'ed means an appointed time or place, and Leviticus 23:2 uses it for the festivals. In verse 6 the LORD has destroyed His 'place of meeting' and made Zion forget the appointed feasts, in verse 7 the enemy shouts in the temple as on a feast day, and in verse 22 He has summoned terrors 'as for the day of an appointed feast.' The BSB renders the Hebrew 'my attackers,' but the original word is magor, 'terror,' the word that Jeremiah made into the name of Pashhur, Magor-missabib, 'terror on every side,' Jeremiah 20:3. The words of the prophet have been fulfilled, and the feast has become a terror.

In verse 14 the visions are 'empty and deceptive.' The Hebrew pairs shav, emptiness, with tafel, a word that Ezekiel 13:10 uses of the whitewash smeared on a flimsy wall. The prophets' message looked solid and was plaster over a wall that would fall.

A single verb carries the chapter's emotional spine: shafak, to pour. The LORD 'poured out His wrath like fire,' verse 4; the poet's heart is 'poured out' in grief, verse 11; and the city is told to 'pour out your heart like water,' verse 19. The same action is wrath, grief and prayer. Psalm 62:8 uses it of trust, and Psalm 22:14 uses it of a sufferer, 'I am poured out like water.'

typology.type: The cut-off horns and the horn of salvation, verses 3 and 17
typology.fulfillment: The poem says that every horn of Israel was cut off and that the horn of her foes was exalted, so that the symbol of David's strength is shattered. Hannah's song had promised that God would exalt the horn of His anointed, 1 Samuel 2:10, and Psalm 132:17 had said that He would make a horn grow for David. In the Gospel, Zechariah announces that God 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. The correspondence rests on the shared image, and the escalation is that the horn is not a king who will be cut off again but a Saviour whose kingdom has no end, Luke 1:33.

typology.type: The scorn of the passers-by, verses 15 and 16
typology.fulfillment: All who pass by clap, hiss and shake their heads, asking, 'Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty?' Psalm 50:2 had called Zion 'perfect in beauty,' and the contempt is the sharper for it. At the crucifixion those who passed by 'heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads,' Matthew 27:39, and mocked the claim that He would destroy and rebuild the temple. The Gospel writer does not quote Lamentations, so this is an echo and not an announced type. The difference is that Jerusalem was mocked for her sin and Christ for bearing it.

typology.type: The silenced law and vision, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The poem says the law is no more and that even the prophets find no vision from the LORD. Amos 8:11 had called it a famine of hearing the words of the LORD. The New Testament says that God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has 'in these last days' spoken by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2, and that the Word became flesh, John 1:14. Where the prophets were silent, the Word is a Person who can be seen and heard. The pattern falls short on one point, since the poem's silence was the result of judgment, whereas the Son speaks in the middle of judgment to bear it.

The one who weeps and the city that is told to pour out its heart anticipate the sufferer of Psalm 22:14, 'I am poured out like water,' a psalm that Jesus took on His lips at the cross. Isaiah 53:12 says that the Servant 'poured out His life unto death,' and Hebrews 5:7 says that Jesus offered prayers 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death.' The poem's instruction to cry out in the night is lived out in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:39. The type falls short because Zion pours out her heart under judgment, while Christ pours out His life for the guilty.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ through its central scene, the cup of God's anger. Isaiah 51:17 says that Jerusalem 'drank from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury,' and Lamentations 2 shows what that looked like: the cloud of anger, the fire in Jacob, the temple abandoned. Isaiah 51:22 then promises, 'From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again.' The question is who drinks it instead. In Gethsemane Jesus prays that this cup might pass from Him and then takes it, Matthew 26:39. The wrath that left Jerusalem in ruins is the wrath that He bears so that Jerusalem need not drink it again.

It leads to Christ through the horn. The poem mourns that every horn of Israel was cut off, verse 3. When Zechariah praises God for the birth of John, he says that God 'has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. The word of the prophets about a restored horn of David, 1 Samuel 2:10 and Psalm 132:17, is carried to Jesus. He is the power of David's house after the house has lost every other power.

It leads to Christ through the temple and the city. Jesus enters Jerusalem and weeps, and He says to it, 'Look, your house is left to you desolate,' Matthew 23:38. In so saying He takes up the very language of this chapter, and He does it as the one who had longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks. The abandonment of the footstool in verse 1 is answered when the veil of the temple is torn in two, Matthew 27:51, and the place where God meets people is no longer a building.

It leads to Christ through the plea for those who suffer. The famished children of verses 11 and 12 and 19 and 20 are held up to God in prayer. The Gospels show Jesus welcoming children, Mark 10:14, and the new Jerusalem is a city where no one hungers any more, Revelation 7:16.

A caution is needed. Zion's anger is the verdict on her own sin, whereas Christ bore wrath for sins that were not His. 2 Corinthians 5:21 says that God made Him 'to be sin on our behalf,' and Galatians 3:13 says He became 'a curse for us.' The chapter is not a prediction of the passion, but it tells the reader exactly what was at stake there, and why only one who was both the Son and a man could carry it.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as holy in a way that is hard to bear. The poem does not soften what He has done: He has covered, cast down, swallowed, demolished, cut off, burned, rejected and delivered over. All of it is said of the LORD, in His own city, against His own people. The central claim of verse 17 is that He 'has done what He planned' and 'accomplished His decree' which He ordained 'in days of old.' Judgment is not a loss of control but the execution of a word spoken beforehand, in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The God of Lamentations 2 is therefore true to His word in the worst way as well as the best. His threats are as dependable as His promises.

It shows God as a God who is not tied to a place. The footstool is abandoned, the sanctuary delivered, the tabernacle laid waste. The LORD allows the temple to fall because the temple was never the guarantee of His presence, a lesson Jeremiah 7:12-14 had taught about Shiloh. This is a hard truth for those who treat holy things as a possession, and a freeing one for those who learn that God cannot be confined to a building and so cannot be lost when the building is.

It shows a God who can be addressed. The poem's prayers are bold: 'Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?' This asks God to compare His own acts with His own character, appealing to the God of Deuteronomy 4:31, who is 'a merciful God' who will not abandon His people. To ask the question is to hold that the answer must be mercy.

It shows a God of justice who sees what the leaders did. The prophets' false visions are named, and the indictment is that they did not expose the people's guilt, verse 14. The LORD is the God who cares about the truth of what is said in His name, Jeremiah 14:14.

For worship, the chapter forbids a shallow faith. It asks the church to hold together a God who judges and a God to whom one may pour out the heart, and it gives words for the moments when the two seem to collide. The worshipper who can say 'Look, O LORD' in the dark has understood that the One who struck is also the only One who can heal, Hosea 6:1.

crossReferences.note: The covenant warned that, if Israel would not listen, they would eat the flesh of their sons and daughters and their cities would be laid waste. Lamentations 2:20 is the fulfilment of that sentence in the starkest verses of the book.

The LORD says He will heap disasters on His people, spend His arrows against them, and let the sword bereave outside while terror strikes within. The picture of bow and arrow in Lamentations 2:4 and the sword in 2:21 is the working out of this song.

The footstool is the place where the ark rests and where Israel worships. When Lamentations 2:1 says that the LORD 'abandoned His footstool,' the poet is saying that He has left the place where He promised to dwell, and that the ark's resting place is empty.

The prophets dress the wound of the people lightly, saying 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace. Lamentations 2:14 looks back on that false message with the weight of the siege behind it and says that such visions were empty.

Ezekiel compares the false prophets to men who whitewash a flimsy wall, and promises it will fall. The same word for whitewash lies behind Lamentations 2:14, which adds to the image of the wall the picture of the wall of Zion that did in fact fall.

Jeremiah renames Pashhur 'Magor-missabib,' terror on every side. Lamentations 2:22 uses the same word when it says the LORD summoned terrors on every side as for a feast day, showing how completely Jeremiah's earlier word became the city's experience.

The Day of the LORD is described as a sacrifice with consecrated guests. The poet's description of the day of anger as a feast to which attackers are summoned in verse 22 is a bitter reversal of the pilgrim festivals that once filled the city.

Jerusalem has drunk the cup of God's fury and staggers. The prophet then says the LORD has taken that cup from her hand and she will never drink it again. Lamentations 2 describes the drinking, and Isaiah describes the end of it.

Zechariah blesses the Lord, who has redeemed His people and raised a horn of salvation in David's house. It is the answer to Lamentations 2:3, where every horn of Israel was cut off. The horn that was lost is given back in a single descendant of David.

Those who pass by at the cross shake their heads and mock the One who would destroy the temple. The scene reads like Lamentations 2:15, where the same gesture of scorn is made at the ruined city, but now the scorn falls on the One who bears the ruin.

A sufferer says 'I am poured out like water,' using the verb that Lamentations 2:19 applies to the heart of the city. The psalm that the Gospels place on Jesus' lips at the cross takes up the image of a heart poured out in prayer.

The prophet calls the people to return to the LORD because He has torn and will heal, wounded and will bind up. It is the answer to 'Who can ever heal you?' in Lamentations 2:13: the One who inflicted the wound is the only One who can heal it.

study.oneStory:
Lamentations 2 is the Bible's picture of what it means for a holy God to live among a sinful people and to take His threats seriously. In Eden the LORD walked in the garden and drove out those who would not trust Him. In the tabernacle He came to live in a tent among Israel, Exodus 25:8, and Solomon's temple was His footstool. The chapter shows the end of that arrangement: the footstool abandoned, the festivals forgotten, the priest and king despised. The long story of God's dwelling with His people has reached its darkest chapter, and the poem insists that He has done it.

It also looks back to the covenant at Sinai. Every verb of destruction in verses 1 to 9 has a source in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, so that the chapter proves the covenant words were not empty. The faithfulness of God is what makes the disaster possible, and it is also what keeps hope alive, because the same God had promised in Deuteronomy 4:31 and 30:1-3 that He would not forget His people in exile.

In what follows, the prophets look past the ruin. Isaiah 51:22 declares that the cup of fury has been taken from Jerusalem. Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD return to a new temple, Ezekiel 43:1-5. And the sufferers of the exile ask the question this poem raises, 'Who can ever heal you?'

The answer comes in Jesus, who pours out His heart in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:39, drinks the cup, and 'poured out His life unto death,' Isaiah 53:12. The veil is torn, the house is left desolate and then rebuilt in three days, John 2:19-21, and the horn of David is raised up. At the end of the story, the city that was once mocked as 'the perfection of beauty' is made new, 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2, and a loud voice declares that the dwelling of God is with men, Revelation 21:3. The footstool abandoned in Lamentations 2:1 is replaced by a throne that the Lamb shares with God.

sermon.title: Suffering in the Believer's Life
sermon.why: Listed on Truth For Life's own collection of Alistair Begg's Lamentations sermons as a message on Lamentations 2:20, this exposition handles the suffering and the cry to God at the heart of this chapter in a faithful, Christ centered way.

quiz.q: What is the most striking claim of Lamentations 2?

options.text: That the Lord Himself, in righteous anger against sin, brought the destruction on Zion and became like an enemy to her.
options.note: The poem makes God the explicit subject of the destruction, 2:1 to 8 and 2:17.

options.text: That God was angry with Jerusalem and judged her.
options.note: True, though it understates how directly and relentlessly the poem names God as the agent.

options.text: That the Babylonians acted entirely on their own against God's will.
options.note: Babylon was the instrument, but the poem insists the Lord ordained and accomplished the judgment.

options.text: That the disaster was a random misfortune with no cause.
options.note: The poem gives it a clear cause: God's just judgment on sin.

quiz.q: What does the chilling refrain without pity, chamal, tell us?

options.text: That God withheld the sparing mercy He normally shows, because persistent, unrepented sin had become so grave.
options.note: Chamal means to spare; its absence measures the seriousness of the sin.

options.text: That God acted without holding back His judgment.
options.note: Correct sense, though it misses that sparing is precisely God's usual way, now withheld.

options.text: That God felt nothing at all about His people.
options.note: The chapter is full of God's engagement; the point is withheld sparing, not indifference.

options.text: That God was cruel and unjust.
options.note: The poem presents the judgment as just, the accomplishing of what He had long decreed.

quiz.q: What does the poet urge the people to do with their grief, in 2:18 to 19?

options.text: To cry out day and night and pour out their hearts like water in the presence of the Lord, lifting up their hands to Him.
options.note: The grief is directed straight back to God in prayer, not away from Him.

options.text: To keep praying and weeping before God without rest.
options.note: True, and specifically to pour out the heart like water and lift hands to Him for the vulnerable.

options.text: To give up on God and accept that all is lost.
options.note: The poem does the opposite: it turns the grief into persistent prayer.

options.text: To take revenge on the Babylonians themselves.
options.note: It calls for crying out to God, leaving judgment to Him.

quiz.q: How does the wound as deep as the sea, Who can ever heal you, point to Christ?

options.text: The incurable wound is healed only in Christ, by whose wounds His people are healed, since God did not spare His own Son.
options.note: The unanswerable question of 2:13 finds its answer at the cross.

options.text: It shows a suffering so deep that only God could heal it.
options.note: True, and Scripture names that healing specifically in Christ's wounds, 1 Peter 2:24.

options.text: It means Jerusalem's wound would never be healed at all.
options.note: The gospel provides the healing the chapter longs for; it is not left hopeless forever.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ.
options.note: The New Testament reads the healing of an incurable wound as fulfilled in Christ.

quiz.q: How can the same God who wounded Zion still be prayed to in this chapter?

options.text: Because the God who justly judged is the only God who can heal, so the poem drives its grief straight to Him.
options.note: Confessing God's hand keeps the sufferer praying rather than despairing.

options.text: Because He is still their God and able to hear their cry.
options.note: True, and more fully because only the God who wounded can also heal.

options.text: Because they hoped God had not really been involved.
options.note: The poem is clear that God was involved; it prays to Him anyway.

options.text: Because prayer here is just empty habit.
options.note: The prayers are urgent and heartfelt, an act of faith that God listens.

questions: This chapter says plainly that God was behind Jerusalem's fall. Is it harder or more comforting for you to believe that nothing, even disaster, falls outside God's hand? Why?
The false prophets comforted the people with visions of peace instead of exposing their guilt. Where are you tempted to prefer reassuring lies over hard truth about your own life?
The poet does not bury his grief or aim it at the enemy; he pours it out like water before the Lord. What would it look like to bring your rawest sorrow directly to God in prayer this week?
Your wound is as deep as the sea, who can ever heal you? Where in your life does the wound feel beyond healing, and how does the cross speak to it?
God did not spare His own Son so that His people would be spared. How does knowing the anger of this chapter fell on Jesus change the way you rest in God's love?

translationNotes.note: His footstool refers to the temple or the ark, the earthly place of God's presence; to abandon His footstool is to give up His own dwelling to destruction.
Every horn can also be rendered all the strength; the horn is a common biblical image of power, so cutting off the horn means breaking Israel's strength.
The opening line is literally Their heart cries out to the Lord; the sense is that the people's hearts cry out, which the translation makes explicit.
The first watch of the night refers to the earliest of the night watches, roughly the hours between six and nine in the evening, the beginning of a whole night of crying out.
